chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Abu al-Bakhtari, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The scholars are the inheritors of the Prophets, and that is because the Prophets did not leave dirhams or dinars as inheritance, but rather they bequeathed narrations from their narrations. So whoever takes something from them has indeed taken an abundant share.

Therefore, look carefully at this knowledge of yours — from whom you take it — for among us, the People of the Household, in every generation there are just ones who repel from it the distortions of the exaggerators, the false attributions of the falsifiers, and the misinterpretations of the ignorant.

key_terms.أَهْلُ الْبَيْتِ: Ahl al-Bayt — the People of the Household (of the Prophet), the Imams and their family
key_terms.انْتِحَالَ الْمُبْطِلِينَ: False attributions of the falsifiers — fabricated narrations or wrongly attributed teachings
key_terms.تَأْوِيلَ الْجَاهِلِينَ: Misinterpretations of the ignorant — incorrect explanations arising from lack of proper knowledge
key_terms.تَحْرِيفَ الْغَالِينَ: Distortions of the exaggerators — alterations introduced by those with extremist views
key_terms.عُدُول: Just ones / upright narrators — used as a rijal term for narrators of established reliability
key_terms.وَرَثَةُ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ: Inheritors of the Prophets — the spiritual and intellectual successors who carry forward prophetic knowledge

ai.seo_question: What does Imam al-Sadiq say about scholars being inheritors of the Prophets?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) declares that scholars are the true heirs of the Prophets, whose legacy consists not of material wealth but of sacred narrations. This hadith emphasises the critical importance of the chain of transmission in Islamic knowledge — particularly that sound religious learning must be taken from the Ahl al-Bayt (the Prophet's household), who in every age safeguard the tradition against three specific corruptions: exaggeration (ghuluww), false attribution (intihāl), and ignorant misinterpretation (ta'wīl). For the early Shi'a community, this hadith functioned as both a theological argument for the Imams' religious authority and a practical directive on where to seek authentic guidance.
